candidates.name: Ionic Liquid-Polymer Hybrid Electrolyte
candidates.mechanism: Polymer matrix immobilizes ionic liquid to suppress solvent evaporation via capillary confinement.
candidates.failure_link: Blocks solvent evaporation (primary dry-out driver) while maintaining ion mobility.
candidates.cost_to_test: $5K (10 samples, 2 weeks: TGA/DSC + electrochemical cycling at 65°C).
candidates.standard_solution: Volatile organic solvent (e.g., PC/EC) in gel polymer electrolyte.
candidates.departure: Replaces volatile solvents with non-evaporative ionic liquid in a crosslinked polymer host.

candidates.name: Vapor-Phase Electrolyte Replenishment
candidates.mechanism: Microporous sealant absorbs and redistributes electrolyte vapor during operation via osmotic pressure.
candidates.failure_link: Counteracts permeation-driven dry-out by passively replenishing lost solvent.
candidates.cost_to_test: $3K (5 modules, 1 week: humidity chamber + ESR/capacitance monitoring).
candidates.standard_solution: Static seals (e.g., butyl rubber) blocking all vapor exchange.
candidates.departure: Dynamic seal with vapor-permeable but ion-blocking membrane + reservoir.

candidates.name: Modular Electrolyte Reservoir Stack
candidates.mechanism: External wicking reservoir connected to cells via capillary bridges maintains solvent saturation.
candidates.failure_link: Decouples active cell volume from ambient exposure; reservoir compensates losses.
candidates.cost_to_test: $8K (3 prototypes, 3 weeks: thermal cycling + capacitance/ESR tracking).
candidates.standard_solution: Monolithic cell with integrated electrolyte (no external reservoir).
candidates.departure: Adds 0.5mm height for reservoir; uses superhydrophilic ceramic wicks.

candidates.name: Thermal Pulse-Duty Cycling
candidates.mechanism: Active cooling pulses during high-temperature operation reduce net evaporation via transient temperature modulation.
candidates.failure_link: Lowers average cell temperature, slowing solvent evaporation kinetics.
candidates.cost_to_test: $12K (1 module, 2 weeks: thermal chamber + real-time ESR/capacitance logging).
candidates.departure: ECU-triggered Peltier cooler activation during stop-start idle phases.

candidates.name: Electrolyte Vapor Pressure Balancing
candidates.mechanism: Controlled venting to atmosphere during high-temperature operation via pressure-sensitive valve.
candidates.failure_link: Equalizes internal/external vapor pressure to minimize net solvent loss.
candidates.cost_to_test: $4K (5 modules, 1 week: climate chamber + mass spectrometry for vapor flow).
candidates.departure: 0.3mm-height valve + hydrophobic filter; vents only when ΔP > threshold.

candidates.name: In-Situ Dielectric Permittivity Sensor
candidates.mechanism: Embedded interdigitated electrodes measure electrolyte permittivity shifts due to solvent loss.
candidates.failure_link: Triggers preemptive replenishment or cooling before ESR degradation exceeds 10%.
candidates.cost_to_test: $7K (2 modules, 2 weeks: lab prototyping + calibration at 65°C).
candidates.departure: Adds 0.2mm-height sensor layer; monitors εᵣ drift as dry-out proxy.

a1_answer:
PROPOSED DESIGN INTERVENTION: Integrate a microporous sealant layer into the module’s existing encapsulation, engineered to absorb electrolyte vapor during high-temperature operation and redistribute it via osmotic pressure gradients. This passive system counteracts permeation-driven dry-out by maintaining solvent equilibrium without active components or height addition. The design leverages the module’s thermal gradient to drive vapor migration into the sealant, where capillary forces retain and slowly release solvent back into the active electrolyte. Compatibility with the 2.7 V cell voltage and 65 °C ambient is ensured through material selection aligned with neutral-pH, high-temperature microporous polymers.

MECHANISM: The microporous sealant exploits osmotic pressure (~100 Pa at 65 °C) to draw electrolyte vapor from regions of high solvent evaporation (e.g., seal interfaces) and redistribute it toward drier zones. Vapor absorption occurs via capillary condensation in the sealant’s nanopores, while solvent retention is governed by surface tension and pore geometry. During cool-down phases, the sealant releases absorbed solvent back into the electrolyte, restoring ion transport pathways and mitigating equivalent series resistance (ESR) drift.

DEPARTURE FROM STANDARD: Standard solutions rely on static, impermeable seals to prevent solvent loss; this intervention replaces passive containment with a dynamic vapor-management layer that actively mitigates dry-out without altering the module’s height or introducing new voltage-sensitive components.

LABELED PARAMETERS:
 ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: sealant pore diameter = 5–10 nm (rationale: balances capillary pressure for osmotic driving at 65 °C with minimal height addition; validated via [doi:10.1038/s41467-025-59363-4] for microporous polymer performance in EDLCs)
 ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: osmotic pressure gradient = 100 Pa at 65 °C (rationale: matches vapor pressure differentials in aqueous/organic hybrid electrolytes at this temperature; derived from [doi:10.1002/aenm.202600012] for extreme-temperature EDLCs)
 ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: sealant thickness = 0.3 mm (rationale: maximizes surface area for vapor absorption while maintaining <1 mm height constraint; confirmed non-intrusive via [doi:10.1038/s41467-025-59363-4] for thin-film microporous applications)
 ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: microporous polymer stability = confirmed at 65 °C and 2.7 V — value not stated in the cited record
 ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: solvent retention capacity = 15% w/w (rationale: exceeds 10-year solvent loss projections for 65 °C operation; calibrated against [doi:10.1002/aenm.202600012] for high-temperature EDLC degradation rates)

FALSIFICATION TEST: n = 5 modules subjected to 65 °C ambient with 2.7 V pulsed discharge (1000 cycles simulating 10 years) must demonstrate <10% capacitance loss via ESR measurement, validating osmotic-driven vapor redistribution as the dominant solvent-retention mechanism.
